screens.title: Advanced Lighting: Lightmapping & Reflection Probes
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll explore two complementary systems that let you get high-quality visuals without killing performance. First, lightmapping: a process that bakes diffuse lighting and shadows into textures so static geometry looks richly lit at runtime without costly per-frame calculations. Second, reflection probes: small environmental captures that supply cubemaps used by metallic and glossy materials to show correct local reflections. Together these tools let you choose where to spend G P U time and where to bake detail ahead of time. You'll learn the three Unity lighting modes — baked, real-time, and mixed — why and when to mark geometry as lightmap static, how to configure lightmap resolution and parameters in the Lighting window, and how to place and bake reflection probes so shiny objects show believable surroundings. A practical activity walks you through baking a room and adding a reflective sphere so you can compare before-and-after results. By the end you'll understand the core trade-offs, the editor steps to create lightmaps and probes, and common mistakes to avoid. As you work, ask yourself which parts of your scene truly need dynamic lighting and which can be baked to save performance.

screens.title: What is Lightmapping?
screens.narratorSegment: Lightmapping is the process of pre-calculating lighting and shadow information and storing that data in textures called lightmaps. These lightmaps are applied to static geometry at runtime so the visual result includes detailed diffuse lighting and soft shadows without the game recalculating them each frame. A concrete example is an indoor room with many static lights and objects: instead of computing hundreds of shadow casts every frame, the lighting for walls, floor, and furniture can be baked once into lightmaps. That saves C P U and G P U work during gameplay and lets you use more complex lighting during authoring. A common misconception is that baked lighting replaces all lighting; it does not. Lightmaps only cover static elements and baked light sources. Dynamic objects still need real-time lighting or mixed lighting so they interact correctly with the scene. In practice you plan which geometry is truly static, mark it as Lightmap Static, and select baked or mixed modes for lights depending on whether you need dynamics. The core insight is that you trade precompute time and storage for much better runtime performance and richer static shadow detail. Try imagining a high-detail interior that maintains 60 frames per second because static light was baked ahead of time.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What is Lightmapping?

Lightmapping

Precompute lighting into textures so static objects show realistic light and shadow without runtime cost.

How it works
  • Render lighting offline for static geometry and store results as lightmap textures.
  • At runtime the renderer samples these textures for diffuse illumination and shadows.
  • Dynamic objects continue to use real-time lighting or mixed modes.
Concrete Example
An indoor studio with many lamps: bake static walls and furniture so shadows are detailed while moving characters remain dynamic.
Analogy: Think of baking as printing a high-resolution poster of the scene's static light.
Misconception
Baked lighting replaces everything — it does not. It only covers static elements and chosen baked lights.
Pro Tip
Start with lower lightmap resolution to iterate quickly, then increase for final output.
Key Takeaway
Bake where geometry is static and expensive to shade each frame.

screens.title: Baked vs Real-time vs Mixed Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing a lighting mode is about trade-offs. Baked lighting precomputes light and shadows into textures and gives the highest visual quality for static scenes with the lowest runtime cost. Use baked lighting when your lights and geometry won't change, such as a staged interior where fixtures and walls are static. Real-time lighting computes light and shadows during gameplay, enabling moving lights and objects to interact correctly, but at a high performance cost; this is essential for dynamic day-night cycles or moving flashlights. Mixed lighting combines both approaches: static objects receive baked lighting while dynamic objects still receive real-time illumination and can cast real-time shadows onto the baked environment. A common misconception is to assume mixed lighting always behaves like full real-time; in reality, mixed lighting attempts to balance fidelity and cost by baking static contributions and leaving dynamics for real-time. When planning, ask which scene elements must respond to changing light. If most of the scene is static, favor baked or mixed to save performance. For small, frequently changing objects, rely on real-time lighting selectively. The final insight: combine modes deliberately to place quality where players will notice it and save cost elsewhere.

keyIdea.title: Mode selection
keyIdea.text: Pick baked for static scenes, real-time for fully dynamic interactions, and mixed when you need both performance and some dynamic response.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Lighting Modes

Baked • Real-time • Mixed

Understand practical trade-offs and when to apply each mode.

Baked Lighting
Pre-calculated, stored in lightmaps, excellent quality for static scenes, lowest runtime cost.
Best for: Interiors, static architecture.
Real-time Lighting
Calculated each frame, required for moving lights/objects, highest performance cost.
Best for: Dynamic gameplay, day-night cycles.
Mixed Lighting
Static objects get baked lighting; dynamic objects interact with real-time lights to preserve some dynamics with less cost than full real-time.
Best for: Mostly static scenes with a few dynamic elements.
Misconception
Mixed lighting is not always a free automatic fix; you must choose which lights are baked or real-time to achieve the intended result.
Key Takeaway
Match the mode to the scene's needs: bake large static areas, use real-time only where necessary.

screens.title: Marking Objects for Lightmapping
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can bake lighting, you need to mark geometry as static for lightmapping. In Unity this is the Lightmap Static flag. Practically, select an object in the Hierarchy, open the Inspector, and set the Static dropdown to include Lightmap Static. Doing this tells Unity the object will not move and its lighting can be precomputed. A helpful workflow is to group your truly static geometry first: walls, floors, ceilings, built-in furniture, and architectural props. Avoid marking characters, doors you plan to animate, or movable props as Lightmap Static; if they are marked static incorrectly they will not respond correctly to runtime dynamics. After marking objects, validate the scene by ensuring only intended objects are static — you can filter the Hierarchy or use layers for clarity. One common mistake is forgetting to set Lightmap Static, which results in the object missing baked lighting and looking out of place. Another practical tip is to mark objects in batches and perform a quick low-resolution bake to confirm selections before committing to long, high-resolution bakes. This saves iteration time and prevents costly re-bakes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Marking Objects

Set Lightmap Static

Tell Unity which objects are static so their lighting can be baked.

Step-by-step
1. Select object(s) in Hierarchy
2. In Inspector open the Static dropdown
3. Enable "Lightmap Static" for selected objects
4. Repeat for all static architecture
Best Practices
  • Group static geometry and mark in batches to avoid mistakes.
  • Don't mark animated or movable props as Lightmap Static.
  • Run a low-resolution bake first to validate selections quickly.
Common Mistake
Forgetting to mark objects as Lightmap Static means they won't receive baked lighting.
Quick Check
Filter the Hierarchy or use grouping to confirm which objects are static before baking.
Key Takeaway
Only mark things that truly never move to ensure correct baked lighting.

screens.title: Configure Lights for Baking
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring your lights correctly matters for both the bake result and performance. In the Inspector for a light you can set the Mode to Baked, Realtime, or Mixed. For purely static illumination — ceiling lamps, static spotlights, or decorative lights — set Mode to Baked. For lights that must move, flicker, or follow characters, use Realtime. Mixed mode is useful when you want static geometry to receive baked lighting while dynamic objects still react to the light; for example, a lamp that stays in place but should cast dynamic shadows from moving characters. The practical steps are: select a light, choose Mode in the Inspector, repeat for all lights that affect the scene. Be mindful of too many realtime lights in complex scenes because they increase per-frame cost. A common misconception is to set all lights to Realtime for convenience; this can severely degrade performance. Instead, decide per-light whether it needs dynamism. After configuring modes, test with a low-resolution bake to check contribution before committing to long bakes. This balances visual fidelity and iteration speed. Configure Lights for Baking means set each light's mode correctly: baked for static, realtime for dynamic, mixed to combine baked static lighting with runtime interaction.. In practical terms, set each light's mode and plan which lights to bake. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Configure Lights

Set Light Modes

Choose per-light whether it should bake or compute at runtime to balance quality and performance.

Inspector Steps
Select Light in Hierarchy
In Inspector find "Mode"
Choose: Baked | Realtime | Mixed
Repeat for each light
When to use each
  • Baked: static fixtures and architecture.
  • Realtime: moving lights and fully dynamic gameplay elements.
  • Mixed: static contribution baked, dynamic objects still update in real time.
Pitfall
Setting everything to Realtime for convenience often results in poor performance.
Key Takeaway
Decide per-light whether it must be dynamic; prefer baked for fixed fixtures.

screens.title: Using the Lighting Window and Bake Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: The Lighting window is where the bake happens. Open it via Window > Rendering > Lighting. In the Scene tab you'll find Lightmap Resolution, Lightmap Parameters, and the Generate Lighting controls. Lightmap Resolution sets the pixel density of your lightmaps: higher resolution gives finer shadow detail but increases file sizes and bake time. Lightmap Parameters control indirect bounces and shadow quality. A practical bake workflow is to disable Auto Generate while iterating, set a low resolution for quick tests, and then increase resolution and refine parameters for the final bake. After adjusting settings click Generate Lighting to start the bake; baking time depends on scene complexity and resolution and can range from seconds to hours. A common misconception is that higher resolution always improves perceived quality; in tight performance budgets it's better to target visible areas with higher resolution and leave distant geometry lower. Also remember to finalize static selections and lights before a long, high-resolution bake. Once baked, inspect the scene for seams, shadow correctness, and whether baked lighting integrates with dynamic objects as expected. Using the Lighting Window and Bake Parameters means use the lighting window to set resolution and parameters; iterate with low-resolution bakes and perform a high-resolution bake for the final output.. In practical terms, adjust resolution, parameters, and generate lighting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Lighting Window

Generate Lighting

Control resolution and quality before running the bake to balance iteration speed and final fidelity.

Open Lighting Window
Menu: Window > Rendering > Lighting
Scene tab → Lightmap Resolution
Scene tab → Lightmap Parameters
Uncheck Auto Generate to iterate manually
Click Generate Lighting to bake
Parameter Guidance
  • Lightmap Resolution: higher = more detail but longer bakes and bigger assets.
  • Lightmap Parameters: control bounces and shadow quality for indirect lighting.
  • Auto Generate: disable for faster iteration control.
Iteration Tip
Use lower resolution for quick visual checks, then increase for the final bake.
Warning
Long final bakes are expected for complex scenes; plan accordingly.
Key Takeaway
Control settings and iterate fast before committing to long bakes.

screens.title: Reflection Probes Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Reflection Probes capture a 360-degree view of their surroundings and store it as a cubemap texture that reflective materials use to simulate local reflections. Unlike lightmaps, which store diffuse lighting, reflection probes provide specular and environment information so metals, glass, and polished surfaces look believable. When a probe is baked it samples the environment inside its bounding box; materials within the probe's influence will sample that cubemap to display reflections. For example, placing a probe in the center of a room and baking it will allow a metallic sphere in that room to reflect nearby walls and objects rather than only the skybox. A common misconception is that lightmaps include reflections — they do not. Without a probe, reflective objects may only reflect a skybox or appear flat. Reflection probes can be Baked, Realtime, or Custom. Baked probes are suitable and efficient for static rooms. Realtime probes update dynamically but are expensive. The practical tip is to use baked probes for most indoor scenes and place probes to cover the areas where reflective materials are used, with slight overlap where necessary to avoid abrupt transitions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Reflection Probes

What is a Reflection Probe?

A probe samples the environment to produce a cubemap that reflective materials use for specular reflections.

Core idea
Reflection probes capture a 360-degree cubemap of a region and supply that data to PBR materials so they reflect local geometry and lighting accurately.
Use baked probes for static rooms; realtime probes for dynamic reflections at higher cost.
Concrete Example
Place a probe in the center of a room and bake. A metallic sphere will now reflect walls and lights in that room instead of only the skybox.
Note: Materials must use Blend Probes or Custom in their Mesh Renderer to receive probe data.
Misconception
Lightmaps do not capture reflections; probes do.
Placement Tip
Scale the probe's bounding box to cover the reflective area; overlap probes slightly where transitions are needed.
Key Takeaway
Use probes to give shiny materials believable, local reflections.

screens.title: Add and Bake a Reflection Probe
screens.narratorSegment: To add a reflection probe use GameObject > Light > Reflection Probe. After creating it, position it roughly where reflections should be accurate and adjust the Box Size and Box Offset so the probe's bounding box covers the intended area. For a typical room place a probe near the room center and scale the box to fill the room. For long corridors you may place multiple probes with slight overlap to avoid abrupt transitions. In the probe's Inspector choose the Type: Baked for static environments, Realtime for dynamic updates, or Custom if you provide your own cubemap. For most static rooms choose Baked and then click Bake in the Inspector to capture the cubemap. Once baked, nearby reflective materials that use Blend Probes or Custom probe usage in their Mesh Renderer will show the probe's reflections. A common oversight is incorrect box size or placement, which leads to reflections that don't match the object's surroundings. Always bake probes after finalizing static geometry and light bakes so the captured cubemap matches the visual state of the scene. Add and Bake a Reflection Probe means add a reflection probe, adjust its bounding box to cover the area, choose baked for static scenes, and click bake to capture the cubemap.. In practical terms, create a probe, size its box, choose type, and bake. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step-by-step Bake

Follow these editor steps to reproduce the room bake and reflective sphere example.

Editor sequence
1. Mark walls/floor/ceiling as Lightmap Static
2. Set Directional Light Mode → Baked

A reflective sphere that shows local room reflections and a baked, high-quality static lighting solution.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.narratorSegment: When working with lightmaps and reflection probes you will encounter a few frequent problems. First, objects that appear to miss baked lighting are often not marked Lightmap Static — check the object's Static dropdown in the Inspector. Second, overly low Lightmap Resolution produces blurry or pixelated shadows; if shadows look blocky, raise resolution or target higher resolution only where players will notice. Third, incorrect reflection probe bounding boxes cause reflections that don't match the object; ensure probes encompass the reflective object area and rebake after changes to static geometry or lighting. Another common issue is forgetting to bake reflection probes after finalizing lights so their cubemap doesn't match the baked lighting. A misconception is to expect probes to update automatically when you rebake lights; baked probes must be baked explicitly. For performance problems, profile with and without baked lighting: baked static areas typically reduce per-frame cost dramatically. When in doubt, run a quick low-resolution bake and a probe bake to verify selections before a long final bake. These checks help you avoid wasted iteration time and produce consistent visual results.

Common Issues & Fixes

Quick diagnosis and corrective actions for common lighting and probe problems.

Missing baked lighting
Ensure objects are marked Lightmap Static. If not, they won't receive baked lightmaps.
Low shadow quality
Increase Lightmap Resolution or adjust Lightmap Parameters to improve shadow detail where visible.
Probe placement errors
Make sure the probe's Box Size covers reflective objects and rebake after changes.
Common Oversight
Not rebaking probes after finalizing static lighting leads to inconsistent reflections.

Compare runtime performance before and after bakes to verify improvements on static-heavy scenes.

screens.title: Combining Baked and Real-time Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: Most complex scenes benefit from a hybrid approach where baked lighting handles the static, costly parts of a scene while real-time lighting addresses dynamic interactions. A practical design pattern is to bake all static architectural and environmental light, then designate a small set of realtime lights for moving characters, weapons, or interactive objects. Mixed lighting is useful when you want static geometry to display baked global illumination but still allow dynamic objects to receive and cast shadows in real time. When planning this architecture, make a list of all moving objects and all lights that must react to them; set those lights to Realtime and leave the rest baked or mixed accordingly. Also plan probe placement so reflective objects still look correct in both static and dynamically lit contexts. The misconception to avoid is assuming more realtime lights always equal better visuals. Instead, aim to place realtime lights strategically where motion and player interaction make a visible difference. This pattern reduces G P U load while preserving important dynamic visual cues for gameplay. Combining Baked and Real-time Lighting means bake environment lighting while reserving real-time lights for moving elements; use mixed mode to blend both where needed.. Combine Baked & Realtime

Use baked lighting for static cost, realtime for moving elements, and mixed mode to bridge them.

Design Pattern
  • Bake static environment and fixtures.

More realtime lights is not always better; place them where dynamics matter most.

Baked large areas reduce runtime cost and free GPU for dynamic effects.

Design lighting around what must be dynamic and what can be baked.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll explore two complementary systems that let you get high-quality visuals without killing performance. First, lightmapping: a process that bakes diffuse lighting and shadows into textures so static geometry looks richly lit at runtime without costly per-frame calculations. Second, reflection probes: small environmental captures that supply cubemaps used by metallic and glossy materials to show correct local reflections. Together these tools let you choose where to spend G P U time and where to bake detail ahead of time. You'll learn the three Unity lighting modes — baked, real-time, and mixed — why and when to mark geometry as lightmap static, how to configure lightmap resolution and parameters in the Lighting window, and how to place and bake reflection probes so shiny objects show believable surroundings. A practical activity walks you through baking a room and adding a reflective sphere so you can compare before-and-after results. By the end you'll understand the core trade-offs, the editor steps to create lightmaps and probes, and common mistakes to avoid. As you work, ask yourself which parts of your scene truly need dynamic lighting and which can be baked to save performance.

These objectives prepare you to both reason about and implement advanced lighting in Unity. First, you'll be able to explain what lightmapping is and why baking lighting into textures benefits performance and visual quality. For example, you'll understand how an indoor scene with many static light sources can keep detailed shadows without expensive per-frame calculations. Second, you'll distinguish between baked, real-time, and mixed lighting modes so you can pick the right approach for moving objects versus static geometry. Third, you'll configure objects for lightmapping — marking them as lightmap static — and then use the Lighting window to set resolution and bake the lightmaps. You'll practice generating a lightmap and learn what resolution and parameters affect quality and bake time. Fourth, you'll understand Reflection Probes: how they capture a cubemap of the environment and how to place, size, and bake probes so metallic surfaces reflect nearby geometry. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the workflow. By the end of the lesson you should be able to plan a bake strategy for a room, run the bake, and add probes so reflective materials integrate visually with the baked scene.

This follow-up objective slide focuses on applying the previous skills with a hands-on task and checking for common mistakes. You'll prepare a simple room scene: mark walls, floor, and static furniture as Lightmap Static and set lights to Baked or Mixed. Then you'll open the Lighting window, adjust lightmap resolution and parameters, and run Generate Lighting to produce baked textures. Once the bake is complete you'll add a reflection probe, size it to the room, and bake the probe so metallic materials show local reflections. The assessment checks that you can choose the correct lighting mode for static versus dynamic objects, and that you remember the key step: marking objects as Lightmap Static before baking. You'll also identify a missing reflection probe when a metallic object looks dull. This objective ties practice to verification and encourages you to compare the baked scene against the pre-bake realtime version to notice performance and visual differences. Use small experiments — only bake at lower resolution first — to iterate faster and avoid unnecessarily long bake times.

Lightmapping is the process of pre-calculating lighting and shadow information and storing that data in textures called lightmaps. These lightmaps are applied to static geometry at runtime so the visual result includes detailed diffuse lighting and soft shadows without the game recalculating them each frame. A concrete example is an indoor room with many static lights and objects: instead of computing hundreds of shadow casts every frame, the lighting for walls, floor, and furniture can be baked once into lightmaps. That saves C P U and G P U work during gameplay and lets you use more complex lighting during authoring. A common misconception is that baked lighting replaces all lighting; it does not. Lightmaps only cover static elements and baked light sources. Dynamic objects still need real-time lighting or mixed lighting so they interact correctly with the scene. In practice you plan which geometry is truly static, mark it as Lightmap Static, and select baked or mixed modes for lights depending on whether you need dynamics. The core insight is that you trade precompute time and storage for much better runtime performance and richer static shadow detail. Try imagining a high-detail interior that maintains 60 frames per second because static light was baked ahead of time.

Choosing a lighting mode is about trade-offs. Baked lighting precomputes light and shadows into textures and gives the highest visual quality for static scenes with the lowest runtime cost. Use baked lighting when your lights and geometry won't change, such as a staged interior where fixtures and walls are static. Real-time lighting computes light and shadows during gameplay, enabling moving lights and objects to interact correctly, but at a high performance cost; this is essential for dynamic day-night cycles or moving flashlights. Mixed lighting combines both approaches: static objects receive baked lighting while dynamic objects still receive real-time illumination and can cast real-time shadows onto the baked environment. A common misconception is to assume mixed lighting always behaves like full real-time; in reality, mixed lighting attempts to balance fidelity and cost by baking static contributions and leaving dynamics for real-time. When planning, ask which scene elements must respond to changing light. If most of the scene is static, favor baked or mixed to save performance. For small, frequently changing objects, rely on real-time lighting selectively. The final insight: combine modes deliberately to place quality where players will notice it and save cost elsewhere.

Before you can bake lighting, you need to mark geometry as static for lightmapping. In Unity this is the Lightmap Static flag. Practically, select an object in the Hierarchy, open the Inspector, and set the Static dropdown to include Lightmap Static. Doing this tells Unity the object will not move and its lighting can be precomputed. A helpful workflow is to group your truly static geometry first: walls, floors, ceilings, built-in furniture, and architectural props. Avoid marking characters, doors you plan to animate, or movable props as Lightmap Static; if they are marked static incorrectly they will not respond correctly to runtime dynamics. After marking objects, validate the scene by ensuring only intended objects are static — you can filter the Hierarchy or use layers for clarity. One common mistake is forgetting to set Lightmap Static, which results in the object missing baked lighting and looking out of place. Another practical tip is to mark objects in batches and perform a quick low-resolution bake to confirm selections before committing to long, high-resolution bakes. This saves iteration time and prevents costly re-bakes.

Configuring your lights correctly matters for both the bake result and performance. In the Inspector for a light you can set the Mode to Baked, Realtime, or Mixed. For purely static illumination — ceiling lamps, static spotlights, or decorative lights — set Mode to Baked. For lights that must move, flicker, or follow characters, use Realtime. Mixed mode is useful when you want static geometry to receive baked lighting while dynamic objects still react to the light; for example, a lamp that stays in place but should cast dynamic shadows from moving characters. Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First: Lightmapping stores precomputed diffuse lighting and shadows in lightmap textures for static geometry, drastically reducing runtime cost for complex indoor scenes. Second: Lighting modes matter — baked lighting delivers the best static quality, realtime lighting supports dynamic interactions, and mixed lighting blends both to give baked static contributions while allowing dynamic objects to receive and cast realtime shadows. Third: Reflection Probes capture cubemaps of their surroundings and supply that data for reflective and metallic materials, which is critical because lightmaps do not provide reflections. Remember to mark static objects as Lightmap Static before baking, use the Lighting window to control resolution and parameters, and bake reflection probes after finalizing static geometry.
